content: Malnutrition is a medical condition that arises from an improper or insufficient diet. It can manifest as undernutrition, which occurs due to inadequate intake, poor absorption, or excessive loss of nutrients. Alternatively, it can also refer to overnutrition, which results from overeating or consuming excessive amounts of specific nutrients. An individual experiences malnutrition when they fail to consume the appropriate quantity or quality of nutrients required for a healthy diet over an extended period. Prolonged malnutrition can lead to starvation, disease, and increased susceptibility to infections. Malnutrition is characterized by a lack of sufficient nutrients necessary to maintain healthy bodily functions. It is often associated with extreme poverty, particularly in economically developing countries, and is a significant cause of reduced cognitive abilities in regions affected by famine. In economically developed countries, malnutrition is frequently observed as a result of inappropriate dieting, overeating, or the absence of a balanced diet. This is often reflected in rising levels of obesity. Most commonly, malnourished individuals either do not consume enough calories or have diets deficient in protein, vitamins, or trace minerals. Medical conditions resulting from malnutrition are referred to as deficiency diseases. Scurvy, caused by a deficiency in vitamin C, is a well-known but now rare example of such a condition. Common forms of malnutrition include protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) and micronutrient malnutrition. PEM occurs when there is insufficient availability or absorption of energy and proteins in the body. Micronutrient malnutrition refers to inadequate levels of essential nutrients, such as vitamins and trace elements, which are required in small quantities. Deficiencies in micronutrients can lead to various diseases and impair the normal functioning of the body. For instance, a deficiency in vitamin A reduces the body's ability to resist infections. Deficiencies in iron, iodine, and vitamin A are widespread and represent significant public health challenges. Nutrient deficiencies are directly linked to a range of adverse effects, including stunted growth, reduced intelligence, impaired cognitive abilities, diminished sociability, lower leadership and assertiveness, decreased physical activity and energy, reduced muscle growth and strength, and overall poorer health. In rare cases, malnutrition can also cause black spots to appear on the skin. Hunger is the natural psychological response triggered by the physiological need for food. It can also affect an individual's mental state and is often used as a metonym for general undernourishment. The causes of malnutrition are diverse and include famine, poverty, digestive diseases, malabsorption, depression, eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, untreated diabetes mellitus, fasting, coma, alcoholism, and certain drug addictions. Overconsumption of fat and sugar, overpopulation, and industrial food processing are also contributing factors. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), between 2001 and 2003, millions of people in various countries were undernourished, consuming less than the minimum amount of food energy required to maintain good health while performing light physical activity. This measure of undernourishment does not account for the additional energy needs of individuals engaged in strenuous physical activity, seasonal variations in food consumption, or individual differences in energy requirements. Malnutrition and undernourishment are cumulative conditions that develop over time and are not the result of a single day's inadequate food intake. Prolonged malnutrition can lead to starvation or deficiency diseases such as scurvy. It may also cause gray discoloration of the nail beds. Malnutrition increases the risk of infections and infectious diseases, such as active tuberculosis. Interestingly, malnutrition has been observed to increase activity and movement in many animals. For example, experiments on spiders have shown that starved spiders exhibit increased activity and predation, leading to greater weight gain. This pattern is also seen in humans during sleep and in animals such as rats, even when their cerebral cortex or stomachs are removed. Increased activity on hamster wheels has been observed in rats deprived not only of food but also of water or B vitamins like thiamine. This response may enhance the animal's chances of finding food, though it has also been speculated that such behavior may relieve pressure on the home population through emigration.
